meta.title: A metallicity-conditioned transformer-based generative model of planetary systems

abstract: Finding exoplanets similar to Earth (Earth twins) is one of the main challenges in exoplanetary science, and the goal of numerous observational surveys. Blind surveys are, however, inefficient in term of observational resources. With numerous new missions planned, leveraging all available information to develop targeted observational strategies, is essential to maximize scientific returns. We extend the character-based generative model framework in [1] by introducing stellar metallicity [Fe/H] as an explicit system-level conditioning variable. This modification enables the model to capture how host star composition influences planetary system configurations and improves predictions on their architectures. The sequence representation encodes stellar metallicity as the initial character, with subsequent characters representing individual planetary properties. We validate the approach on observed multi-planet systems by hiding all planets except one and attempt at inferring the distribution of properties of the remaining planets. We test the system presented in [1] (TOI 469) as well as two additional systems initially discovered by the TESS satellite [2] and further characterized by CHEOPS [3] (TOI 836 and TOI 1064). Results demonstrate that the model successfully predicts the properties of hidden planets and that conditioning on host star metallicity produces more constrained posterior distributions.

blocks.html: Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in areas such as planetary sciences and exoplanet detection. Current missions such as CHEOPS [3] and facilities as ESPRESSO [4] have greatly improved our ability to find small planets. Upcoming observational surveys like PLATO [5] aim at improving the detection and characterization of low-mass exoplanets, and future facilities like LIFE [6] aim at finding potentially habitable worlds. However, searching the entire sky without a prioritization strategy is inefficient. Observational strategies are therefore needed to identify key systems, allowing for more effective use of resources.

Planetary systems show organized structures with correlated properties. The "peas-in-a-pod" pattern [7, 8] is a striking example: planetary properties are not independent but reflect the system’s formation history and evolution. These correlations can be used to predict whether undetected planets exist in alreadyobserved systems. Additionally, stellar properties, like metallicity [Fe/H] impact the architecture of the planetary systems. The metallicity is the amount of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium - [Fe/H] represents the ratio of iron to hydrogen, normalized to the solar value, in a log scale. It has been shown for instance, that giant planets occur more frequently around high metallicity stars [9]. As such, metallicity is a property of the system as a whole, which raises the question of how such a global scalar should enter a model that generates planets sequentially.

While population synthesis models [10] provide realistic predictions, they are computationally expensive for large-scale observational planning. Recent machine learning methods have shown promise for understanding exoplanet systems through statistical and classification methods [11, 12]. Yet, these approaches rely on simplifying assumptions, notably treating planets as conditionally independent given the system, which limits their accuracy. Treating a planetary system as a sequence of planets instead allows the correlations described above to be modelled directly.

In [1], a transformer-based approach is proposed to generate planetary systems that capture inter-planetary correlations at low computational cost. In the present work, we extend this approach by adding the stellar metallicity as a system-level property to help refine the architecture of the generated systems. We deliberately retain the model architecture of [1], so that the effect of conditioning on the stellar property is isolated, and instead modify how system-level information enters the model at an encoding level: metallicity is injected as an additional token in the beginning of the word, selected from an independent vocabulary set. We validate its impact by testing on real systems observed by CHEOPS and TESS, where we show that stellar metallicity conditions the distribution of properties of yet-undetected planets. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 describes the data, encoding strategies and impact on the training, Section 3 the tests and evaluation using real systems and Section 4 concludes.

The Bern model [10] is a population synthesis global model that simulates planetary system formation and evolution. Several physical processes are included such as: planetary core growth (by accretion of km-sized planetesimals), disc-driven migration (movement of planets due to interactions with the protoplanetary disc), gravitational interactions between planets (Nbody dynamics), and the long-term cooling and contraction of planets after formation. It produces populations of synthetic systems by varying initial disc properties and planetary embryo characteristics based on observed distributions.

We reuse the dataset in [1] produced with the Bern model and consisting of approximately 25,000 synthetic systems with up to 20 planets each orbiting solar mass stars. Host star metallicity can be deduced from the protoplanetary disc properties for each system.

The generative model is a simplified transformer [13], adapted for character-level token generation of planetary systems: each system is represented as a sequence of discrete tokens encoding planetary properties. This architecture has already been shown to capture interplanet dependencies and system-level correlations between planetary properties efficiently [1], which makes it well suited to probabilistic inference and to predicting missing planets in partially observed systems.

While other simpler sequence models, such as recurrent networks, are often competitive, the choice of a transformer is well justified. Two features of the problem favour attention. The first is that the correlations we want to reproduce link planets that are far apart in the sequence: attention connects any two planets directly, while a recurrent network has to pass that information along through every planet in between. The second is that metallicity describes the system rather than an individual planet. Because every position attends to the full sequence, a system-level property encoded once is equally available to the innermost and the outermost planet; a recurrent network instead carries it in a hidden state that is overwritten at each step, so its effect fades along the sequence. This matters when we generate new systems at a chosen metallicity, since the star should shape the whole system and not only its first few planets. It also explains why the encoding is the natural place to intervene: a global property can be made visible to the whole sequence without altering the model itself. Keeping the architecture of [1] unchanged is a further deliberate choice, since any improvement can then be attributed to the stellar conditioning rather than to a different model.
As such, retain that architecture exactly as published in [1]. Our contribution lies in the encoding, where stellar metallicity is introduced as a system-level property of the token sequence.

A planetary system is encoded as a token sequence x = (x1, x2, . . . , xn), where the token x1 represents the system property (metallicity [Fe/H]) and the others xi represent individual planetary properties (semi-major axis and mass). The system and planetary properties use disjoint vocabularies to avoid token ambiguity. Moreover, positional encoding is not applied, as planetary positions within the system are implicitly determined by tokens.

blocks.html: In this work, a word corresponds to a planetary system where the first character encodes the stellar metallicity [Fe/H] and the following characters encode individual planets properties as illustrated in Fig.1. Host star metallicity is encoded independently using a onedimensional grid with 50 discrete characters distributed uniformly in logarithmic metallicity space. The planetary properties are encoded following the approach of [1], i.e. using a 30×30 discrete two-dimensional grid in logarithmic mass and semi-major axis space.

The benchmark model achieved a test loss of 2.39, much lower than the random baseline loss of 5.97 (for vocabulary sizes V1 = 47 and V2 = 440), indicating effective learning of planetary system representations. The analysis of generated words reveals no evidence of direct memorization from the training dataset. Among the generated sequences, only ∼4.3% contain construction errors, defined as incorrect character placement or selection from an inappropriate vocabulary set for that token position. This low error rate indicates robust learning of the encoding constraints.

The individual and joint probability distributions of generated systems closely match the corresponding distributions of the training data. However, the approach inherits from the limitation noted in [1]: the discretization of continuous parameter space onto a finite grid introduces information loss. This discretization limits the precision with which continuous planetary properties can be represented and reconstructed. We apply the stability criterion in [1] derived from [14] and we obtain similar results on the generated planetary systems, meaning that the introduction of stellar metallicity does not compromise stability.

We start by applying the metallicity-conditioned model to the system TOI-469 (properties in Table 1) and evaluate the predictions with and without stellar metallicity as conditioning variable. The metallicity of each system is allowed an uncertainty of 20% to account for observational measurement uncertainties. We filter generated sequences to retain only those containing planet b (allowing a 10% uncertainty in mass and 1% uncertainty in semi-major axis) and use this singleplanet constraint to predict the posterior probability distributions of mass and semi-major axis for unobserved planets (planets c and d for this system). We generated 500,000 stable systems, from which 125 contain a planet with properties matching TOI-469 planet b like. Imposing the stellar metallicity constraint reduces these to 30 systems. The joint distributions for the obtained systems are displayed in Fig. 2.

blocks.html: The inclusion of stellar metallicity as a conditioning variable produces improvements in prediction accuracy. Without metallicity, the generated results combine diverse system architectures, including configurations with warm Jupiters as well as systems composed entirely of smaller, lower-mass planets like peas-in-a-pod strain, the predicted distributions narrow substantially to favour systems with only lower-mass planets (Fig. 2b), a configuration consistent with the observed properties of the TOI-469 system. This architectural discrimination demonstrates that stellar metallicity can be used effectively to distinguish between fundamentally different system types, even when other orbital parameters are not fully constrained.

blocks.html: In Figure 3, we extend the validation to two additional observed systems: TOI-836 and TOI-1064. These systems were also firstly observed by TESS and then characterized with CHEOPS. Their properties are also displayed in Table 1. For the first system (TOI- 836), conditioning on the stellar metallicity improves the prediction of the mass for planet c compared to the unconstrained model, but provides no additional refinement of the semi-major axis distribution. For the second system (TOI-1064), taking into account the stellar metallicity leads to a narrower distribution for both mass and semi-major axis distributions. Interestingly, planet c, in this latter case, is better reproduced by the model.

These results indicate that while metallicity conditioning effectively constrains certain planetary configurations, its utility depends strongly on the system architecture and whether such configurations are adequately represented in the training population.

This work extends a transformer-based generative model for exoplanet prediction by incorporating stellar metallicity as an explicit system-level conditioning variable. We demonstrated that the model successfully learns to generate diverse planetary system configurations while constraining predictions based on host star composition.

Testing on the reference system from [1] revealed that metallicity conditioning effectively distinguishes between fundamentally different architectures—specifically, constraining predictions away from warm Jupiter configurations toward systems of purely lower-mass planets consistent with TOI-469. Validation on two additional observed systems revealed nuanced results. For TOI-836, metallicity conditioning improved mass predictions while leaving semi-major axis distributions largely unchanged. However, for the second additional system (TOI-1064), stellar metallicity conditioning demonstrated refining both mass and semi-major axis distributions such that the observed planet c position now lies within the constrained posterior distribution. This finding highlights both the power and limitations of the approach: while metallicity clearly encodes information about planetary system composition and architecture, its utility is constrained by the statistical coverage of the underlying training data.

This work establishes a foundation for several promising avenues of investigation. The current approach conditions only on stellar metallicity, though host star age, stellar activity, and disk properties also influence planetary system architectures but are not yet incorporated. Systematic exploration of additional system-level conditioning variables could substantially enhance predictive power. To conclude, as exoplanet surveys expand to characterize increasingly diverse systems, such conditioning strategies will become essential for optimizing observational prioritization and extracting maximum scientific value from limited observational resources.
